statement: Genesis 6–9 was shaped within a Mesopotamian flood-story tradition in which Atraḫasīs is a particularly important precursor; John Day argues the non-P/Yahwist account is closer to Atraḫasīs than to Gilgamesh, while David Carr argues both pre-P and Priestly flood narratives were modeled on earlier Mesopotamian flood traditions especially represented by Atraḫasīs and Gilgamesh XI.

sources.citation: John Day, “Comparative Ancient Near Eastern Study: The Genesis Flood Narrative in Relation to Ancient Near Eastern Flood Accounts,” in Biblical Interpretation and Method (Oxford University Press, 2013), pp. 74–88.
sources.author: John Day
sources.access_note: Oxford abstract says the Yahwist account is closer to Atraḫasīs, itself the source of the Gilgamesh version, and discusses direct versus indirect Mesopotamian dependence.

sources.citation: David M. Carr, The Formation of Genesis 1–11: Biblical and Other Precursors (Oxford University Press, 2020), ch. 6, “Precursors to the Flood Narrative (Gen 6:5–9:17).”
sources.author: David M. Carr
sources.access_note: Oxford abstract states that both the pre-P and Priestly flood narratives appear modeled on earlier Mesopotamian flood traditions, especially Atraḫasīs and Gilgamesh XI.

does_not_demonstrate: This does not prove direct access to a specific Atraḫasīs manuscript.
This does not exclude mediation through Gilgamesh, oral circulation, or other Mesopotamian flood traditions.
This does not mean every feature of Genesis 6–9 derives from Mesopotamia.
adversarial_counter: The exact transmission chain is undocumented; Atraḫasīs, Gilgamesh XI, and wider Mesopotamian flood tradition may all stand behind different features of Genesis.
notes: Backs a CULTURAL_FUSION/MODERATE edge rather than a direct BORROWING claim.
